items.followUp: Name any two highly reactive metals.

rubric.why: One correct example earns credit for the first metal.
rubric.description: Names one moderately reactive metal.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for any one of zinc, iron, lead or copper.

rubric.why: A second correct example completes the response.
rubric.description: Names a second, different moderately reactive metal.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a different correct metal from the first.

modelAnswer: Zinc and iron are two moderately reactive metals.

items.followUp: Write the names of any two low-reactivity metals.

rubric.why: The balanced equation shows the chemical reaction of magnesium with oxygen.
rubric.description: Writes the balanced chemical equation.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO.

rubric.why: The observation describes the characteristic product and burning of magnesium.
rubric.description: States an observation or identifies the product.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the dazzling white flame or formation of white magnesium oxide.

modelAnswer: Magnesium burns in oxygen with a dazzling white flame.
A white powder of magnesium oxide is formed.
2Mg(s) + O₂(g) → 2MgO(s)

rubric.why: Sodium is used in lamps that produce a bright yellow light.
rubric.description: Gives one use of sodium in sodium-vapour lamps.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for sodium-vapour lamps or street lighting.

rubric.why: Liquid sodium can transfer heat in nuclear reactors.
rubric.description: Gives a second use of sodium as a reactor coolant.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for use as a coolant in nuclear reactors.

modelAnswer: Sodium is used in sodium-vapour lamps for street lighting.
Liquid sodium is used as a coolant in nuclear reactors.

items.followUp: Compare the electronic configurations of sodium and magnesium and state which is more reactive.

rubric.why: Sodium has one electron in its outermost shell.
rubric.description: Gives sodium's electronic configuration or one valence electron.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the configuration 2,8,1 or the statement that sodium has one outer-shell electron.

rubric.why: The comparison identifies magnesium's two outer-shell electrons and why it is less readily oxidised.
rubric.description: Compares magnesium's outer shell with sodium's.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the configuration 2,8,2 or the statement that magnesium has two outer-shell electrons and loses them less readily.

modelAnswer: Sodium has the electronic configuration 2,8,1, whereas magnesium has 2,8,2.
Sodium loses its single outermost electron more readily; magnesium has a greater nuclear charge and holds its outer electrons more strongly.
Therefore, sodium is more reactive than magnesium.

items.followUp: State the main postulates of Rutherford's atomic model.

rubric.why: This states the basic arrangement of electrons in Bohr's model.
rubric.description: States that electrons revolve around the nucleus in definite orbits.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for electrons revolving around the nucleus in circular or definite orbits.

rubric.why: Each permitted orbit has a particular energy.
rubric.description: States that each orbit has a fixed energy.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that an orbit or shell has a definite energy.

rubric.why: This is a key distinction of Bohr's stationary orbits.
rubric.description: States that an electron does not radiate energy while in a permitted orbit.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that electrons do not emit or radiate energy while remaining in an orbit.

rubric.why: Energy is exchanged when an electron changes its orbit.
rubric.description: Describes absorption or emission during an electron transition.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that an electron absorbs energy to move to a higher orbit or emits energy to move to a lower orbit.

rubric.why: The energy exchanged corresponds to the difference between the two energy levels.
rubric.description: Relates the energy exchanged to the difference between the orbits.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the energy absorbed or emitted equals the energy difference between the two orbits (ΔE = hν).

modelAnswer: Electrons revolve around the nucleus in fixed circular paths called orbits or shells.
Each permitted orbit has a definite, fixed energy.
An electron does not emit or absorb energy while it remains in a permitted orbit.
An electron absorbs energy to jump to a higher-energy orbit and emits energy when it falls to a lower-energy orbit.
The energy absorbed or emitted equals the difference between the energies of the two orbits: ΔE = hν.

items.followUp: Classify molecules by the number of atoms and give one example of each type.

rubric.why: A monoatomic molecule contains one atom.
rubric.description: Names the monoatomic type and gives an example.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for monoatomic with an example such as helium.

rubric.why: A diatomic molecule contains two atoms.
rubric.description: Names the diatomic type and gives an example.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for diatomic with an example such as H₂ or O₂.

rubric.why: A triatomic molecule contains three atoms.
rubric.description: Names the triatomic type and gives an example.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for triatomic with an example such as water or ozone.

rubric.why: A polyatomic molecule contains more than three atoms.
rubric.description: Names the polyatomic type and gives an example.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for polyatomic with an example such as P₄ or S₈.

modelAnswer: Monoatomic molecules contain one atom, for example helium (He).
Diatomic molecules contain two atoms, for example oxygen (O₂).
Triatomic molecules contain three atoms, for example water (H₂O).
Polyatomic molecules contain more than three atoms, for example phosphorus (P₄).

items.followUp: Define dipole-dipole forces and state how they affect boiling points.

rubric.why: The definition identifies the hydrogen attraction and the electronegative atoms involved.
rubric.description: Defines hydrogen bonding and identifies the atoms involved.
rubric.how: Award 2 marks for describing attraction between H bonded to a highly electronegative atom (N, O or F) and a lone pair on another such atom; award 1 mark for a partly correct definition.

rubric.why: Hydrogen bonds require extra energy to overcome, raising phase-change temperatures.
rubric.description: States that hydrogen bonding raises melting or boiling points.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that hydrogen bonding raises the melting point or boiling point.

rubric.why: Strong attractions between molecules affect resistance to flow and the liquid surface.
rubric.description: States an effect on surface tension or viscosity.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that hydrogen bonding increases surface tension or viscosity.

rubric.why: Hydrogen bonding creates an open structure in ice.
rubric.description: Explains the unusual density of ice compared with liquid water.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that ice is less dense than liquid water because of its hydrogen-bonded structure.

modelAnswer: Hydrogen bonding is the intermolecular attraction between a hydrogen atom covalently bonded to a highly electronegative atom (N, O or F) and a lone pair on an electronegative atom of a neighbouring molecule.
These attractions are relatively strong, so extra energy is needed to separate the molecules; consequently, hydrogen bonding raises melting and boiling points.
It also increases properties such as surface tension and viscosity.
In ice, hydrogen bonds form an open structure, making ice less dense than liquid water.

items.followUp: Define boiling and state three factors that affect the boiling point of a liquid.

rubric.why: The definition describes molecules escaping from the liquid surface into the gas phase.
rubric.description: Defines evaporation.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing the change of a liquid into vapour from its surface, below its boiling point.

rubric.why: Higher temperature gives molecules more energy, and a larger surface exposes more molecules to escape.
rubric.description: Identifies temperature and/or surface area as factors.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that evaporation increases with higher temperature or greater surface area.

rubric.why: Moving air removes vapour, while humid air slows further evaporation.
rubric.description: Identifies wind speed and/or humidity as factors.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that evaporation increases with wind speed or decreases with humidity.

rubric.why: Different liquids have different strengths of attraction between their particles.
rubric.description: Identifies the nature of the liquid as a factor.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that evaporation depends on the liquid's nature or intermolecular forces.

modelAnswer: Evaporation is the escape of molecules from the surface of a liquid to form vapour, at a temperature below the boiling point.
Higher temperature increases evaporation because more molecules have enough energy to escape.
A larger surface area increases evaporation.
Higher wind speed increases evaporation, while higher humidity decreases it.
The nature of the liquid also matters: liquids with weaker intermolecular forces evaporate more readily.
